---
title: "Class 10. Rosling assembly, 2007 (solutions)"
format: html
---

**Question for today:** What is the link between income and life expectancy in 2007?

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, here)
```

Rosling shows four variables at once: x is income, y is life expectancy, size is population, color is continent. We build the chart one layer at a time.

## 1. Start: two numbers

```{r}
#| label: step-1
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point()
```

## 2. Log scale on x

Income spans 278 to 49,357 dollars. A linear axis squeezes most countries to the left. A log axis gives each doubling the same width.

```{r}
#| label: step-2
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```

## 3. Size by population

`scale_size_area()` makes the area of each circle proportional to population, which is honest. The default radius scale exaggerates differences.

```{r}
#| label: step-3
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15)
```

## 4. Color by continent

`alpha = 0.7` makes circles see-through, so overlaps stay visible.

```{r}
#| label: step-4
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15)
```

## 5. Axis number format

`scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)` adds the dollar sign and the thousands separator. Put it inside the existing `scale_x_log10()`. A second `scale_x_log10()` would replace the first one.

```{r}
#| label: step-5
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15)
```

## 6. Colors that everyone can read: viridis (about 15 minutes)

The default ggplot2 colors are hard to tell apart for people with color blindness, and some turn to the same gray in a black and white printout. The viridis palettes fix both. They ship with ggplot2.

- `scale_color_viridis_d()`: for categories (`d` = discrete).
- `scale_color_viridis_c()`: for numbers (`c` = continuous).

```{r}
#| label: viridis-d
# Categories: continent
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_viridis_d()
```

```{r}
#| label: viridis-c
# Numbers: color by life expectancy itself
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population, color = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_viridis_c()
```

**Question:** Which of the three versions (default, `_d`, `_c`) can you read in a black and white printout? Why does color by `life_exp` repeat the y axis, and when is that useful?

Answer: the viridis versions keep an order of dark to light that survives gray printing. The default colors share similar gray values. Color by `life_exp` repeats the y axis, which adds no new information here; use it when a third number has no axis.

**Your turn:** Try `scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.9)`. What does `end = 0.9` do?

```{r}
#| label: turn-viridis
here("data", "rosling_tidy.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = life_exp, size = population, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.9)
```

Answer: `end = 0.9` stops the palette before its lightest color, so the last category stays visible on a white background.

> Deliverable: the static Rosling chart for 2007 with four variables, dollar labels and a viridis palette.
